newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny moves across tip of Louisiana.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny moves across tip of Louisiana.

text.p: Tropical Storm Danny strengthened to a hurricane early Friday as it swept across Louisiana's southeastern tip.
The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said Danny just made it into the hurricane category with top sustained winds of about 75 mph (120 kph).
From a position about 40 miles (65 km) south-southeast of New Orleans at 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), Danny was expected to drift slowly north-northeast, the centre said.
Its track took it onto the 65-mile-long (104-km) peninsula that locals call Louisiana's toe and put Alabama in its sights for the weekend.
Danny had sustained winds of 60 mph (96 kph) when it moved ashore late Thursday after languishing most of the day off the Louisiana coast, meteorologists said.
A hurricane watch was issued for an area from Morgan City in central Louisiana to Destin, Florida, in the Florida panhandle.

Rains up to four inches (10 cm) were reported Thursday night, but the slow-moving storm was expected to dump up to 10 inches (25 cm) of rain as it lumbered across land. There were no reports of damage, although there was moderate flooding in some areas.

At Grand Isle, 60 miles (96 km) south of New Orleans, long lines of cars formed on Louisiana Highway 1 as the area's 1,500 residents evacuated ahead of Danny. Officials said the highway -- the only way off the island -- would be flooded by a five-foot (1.5-metre) storm surge.
"The main reason I ordered everybody out is because we got plenty tourists on the island and I don't want nobody stuck here," Grand Isle Mayor Arthur Bellanger told Reuters.
Evacuations were also ordered in parts of Terrebonne and Lafourche parishes southwest of New Orleans, but people in some areas began returning to their homes Thursday night as the storm went east.
In low-lying St. Bernard Parish, southeast of New Orleans, officials handed out sandbags to seal off flood-prone roads and recommended that residents leave.

"If we get an east or northeast wind, it could really push some water into parts of the parish outside of the hurricane protection levees," Mike Sanders, spokesman for the St. Bernard Parish sheriff's department, said.

In New Orleans, late-night revellers on Bourbon Street barely broke stride as light rains and intermittent gusts swept the historic French Quarter. Even though officials had feared flooding in the city, which is below sea level, Danny hit the Big Easy with a weak punch.
Mayor Marc Morial said city offices would open Friday, as usual.
